previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with chronic pancreatitis, depression, anxiety, and a history of venous thrombosis, was admitted for an acute exacerbation of chronic pancreatitis characterized by severe epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and inability to tolerate oral intake. She was managed with IV fluids, IV pain medications including Toradol and Dilaudid, and antiemetics per her established outpatient protocol. Her symptoms gradually improved, allowing transition to oral tramadol and a regular diet. Blood pressure was elevated on admission, likely due to pain and missed medications, and was managed by restarting lisinopril and increasing amlodipine from 5mg to 10mg daily. IV pantoprazole was used temporarily and switched back to oral omeprazole. She remained mentally stable on home seroquel and amitriptyline. She was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up instructions for blood pressure monitoring and primary care.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with pancreatitis / chronic pain, no IV access 
// place picc (per ___ team, bedside placement failures in past)

COMPARISON:  ___

TECHNIQUE:  OPERATORS: Dr. ___, Interventional Radiology Fellow and Dr.
___, attending radiologist performed the procedure. Dr. ___
personally supervised the trainee during the entire procedure and has reviewed
and agrees with the trainee's findings.
ANESTHESIA: 1% lidocaine was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues
overlying the access site.
MEDICATIONS: None
CONTRAST: 3 ml of Optiray contrast.
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE:  1.5 min, 20 cGy

PROCEDURE:
1. Double lumen PICC placement through the brachial vein on the right.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Using sterile technique and local anesthesia, the basilic
vein on the right was punctured under direct ultrasound guidance using a
micropuncture set. Permanent ultrasound images were obtained before and after
intravenous access, which confirmed vein patency. A peel-away sheath was then
placed over a guidewire. The guidewire was then advanced into the superior
vena cava using fluoroscopic guidance. A double lumen PIC line measuring 42 cm
in length was then placed through the peel-away sheath.  It was not
obstruction noted at the level of the axillary vein.  The PICC was then pulled
back and contrast was injected through the lumen.  A venogram was performed. 
The PICC was then removed and cut to a length measuring 16 cm.  The PICC was
advanced through the sheath with its tip positioned in the axillary vein under
fluoroscopic guidance. Position of the catheter was confirmed by a
fluoroscopic spot film of the chest. The peel-away sheath and guidewire were
then removed. The catheter was secured to the skin, flushed, and a sterile
dressing applied.
The patient tolerated the procedure well. There were no immediate
complications.

FINDINGS: 

1.  The accessed left deep brachial vein was patent and compressible.
2.  Occlusion of the right axillary vein with collaterals opacifying more
central veins.
2.  Brachialvein approach single lumen right PICC with tip in the axillary
vein.

IMPRESSION: 

Successful placement of a right 16 cm brachial approach double lumen PowerPICC
with tip in the axillary vein.  The line is ready to use.

RECOMMENDATION(S):  For future RUE picc, patient will require axillary
venoplasty (Prev hx of Lt UE DVT)
